name: PT Bukit Uluwatu Villa Tbk

frontmatter.title: Bukit Uluwatu Villa: a Bali luxury portfolio priced as a development option
frontmatter.summary: We initiate at REDUCE with a twelve-month target of Rp269, a return of -14.2% from Rp314. The Bali luxury portfolio and the rights-funded Uluwatu and Bintan pipeline are real, but the last profit was an associate land-sale gain and the shares trade at 3.10 times our fundamental value. The lens is a deck assumption, not sourced group support; the bear-regime target is Rp159.
thesis: FY2025's profit was a one-off: the associate line booked the gain on the Labuan Bajo land and hotel sale, while operating profit fell on higher G&A; we do not capitalise that gain.

The October rights issue recapitalised the balance sheet and retires the Mandiri facility, but it also increased the share count by a quarter; we carry the development land at its funded cost, not at the option value the price pays.
The four trading hotels are a small, genuinely premium Bali portfolio with high room rates and occupancy that slipped; on their own cash flow the equity is worth a fraction of the market value.

The price is a konglo premium, not a fundamentals call: the name is group-controlled but not on the HSC list, sits comfortably above the free-float floor, and the lens keeps only part of the gap. That lens is the deck's flag-based regime calculation, not a claim that the group supports the price.
Even the modelled bull case, which assumes on-time development conversion and a demand recovery, stays below today's price; the risk-reward is skewed to the downside.

catalysts.event: Allotment of the remaining HMETD and the final post-exercise share count and free float
Early repayment of the Bank Mandiri facility from rights-issue proceeds, targeted for late November
Targeted closing of the RUR acquisition and the West Resort land transfer
FY2026 results and the first full-year test of the company's revenue and profit budget
Exchange free-float rule takes effect for large caps (sector-wide)
Deadline for feedback in the MSCI Standalone consultation (sector-wide)
MSCI decision on Indonesia's market classification (sector-wide)
Targeted completion of Uluwatu Estate infrastructure
Targeted completion of the West Resort development

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of PT Bukit Uluwatu Villa at **REDUCE** with a twelve-month target of **Rp269**, an expected total return of **-14.2%** from the last close of Rp314 [S0]. The target is the konglo deck's most likely twelve-month price, not an instant convergence to value: our probability-weighted twelve-month fundamental is Rp113, the price sits at 3.10 times the current fundamental value of Rp101, and the lens closes 30.0% of the log gap over the year while keeping the rest [S0]. The call is not a rejection of the assets. It is a statement about what the market already pays for them.

The company owns and operates a small luxury portfolio: four hotels, 301 rooms, five restaurant and bar units and a land bank of 40.20 hectares anchored in Uluwatu, Bali [S3/F3][S3/F4][S3/F5][S3/F6]. FY2025 revenue was IDR375.6bn, EBITDA IDR109.2bn and attributable profit IDR99.2bn, but the profit line is not an operating number: the associate line contributed IDR79.4bn from the sale of the Labuan Bajo land and hotel project for IDR799.1bn, while operating profit fell 8.1% as general and administrative costs rose [S2/F11][S2/F12][S3/F65]. Strip the gain out and the hotel business earned roughly what it earned the year before.

Our variant view is that the market is paying for a development option, not for the current cash flow. On the four trading hotels' own cash flow, the equity is worth Rp113 a share; the price implies revenue growth of 28.0% in the first forecast year, against our 5.0% base, and capitalises the development land far above the cash committed to it [S0][S4]. We carry the October rights-issue proceeds of IDR1,538.6bn and the development land at book of IDR621.0bn in the valuation bridge. The record does contain sourced market marks for individual parcels - the Labuan Bajo land and hotel sale and the RUR West Resort land - but they are specific transactions with different permissions and development status, so we use cost as the base and do not put a per-hectare mark-up in the model; even the bull case carries the land at book [S2/F12][S4/F26][S4/F30].

What moves the value. First, conversion: Uluwatu Estate infrastructure is due by Q4 2028 and West Resort by Q4 2029, and the company has not disclosed room counts, rates or returns for either [S4/F53][S4/F54]. Second, demand: foreign arrivals to Bali fell 1.6% in the year to August while national arrivals rose 5.4%, so the destination is underperforming the country [S9/F46][S10/F49]. Third, the regime: the price is a konglo premium, and the lens, not our DCF, translates it into the target [S0]. The rights issue retires the Mandiri facility and funds the pipeline, but it also increases the share count by a quarter and leaves 1.88bn HMETD to the standby buyers [S4/F20][S4/F23][S5][S12/F71].

Bali's luxury resort market is a destination business in which scarcity of land in the south of the
island, brand management and airlift matter more than scale. The listed Indonesian hotel owners are
mostly small relative to the global operators whose brands they carry, and many sit inside family
conglomerates with concentrated control, so the traded price can reflect group capital-markets
activity as much as the cash flow of the rooms.

PT Bukit Uluwatu Villa was established at the end of 2000 and began developing Alila Villas Uluwatu in 2006, opening the resort in 2009; it listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange in 2010 and has been controlled by PT Nusantara Utama Investama since the middle of 2023 [S3]. Its operating model is simple to state and hard to scale: it develops and owns trophy resort assets, usually under the Alila luxury brand and its associated management arrangements, and it sells villas and land at the margin through a small real-estate segment [S2][S3].

The portfolio at the end of FY2025 comprised four hotels in operation — two owned directly by the company, one owned by a subsidiary and one owned through an indirect subsidiary interest — with 301 rooms, five restaurant and bar units and 40.20 hectares of land bank [S3/F3][S3/F4][S3/F5][S3/F6]. The named assets are Alila Villas Uluwatu, Alila Ubud, Alila Manggis and the Dialoog Banyuwangi hotel, with Alila Ubud alone accounting for 74 rooms [S3/F39]. The group also holds interests through associates: the associate profit sits entirely inside the hotel segment in the audited segment note, alongside the consolidated hotels [S2][S3].

Revenue mix follows the rooms. Hotel and villa revenue was IDR229.2bn in FY2025, with restaurants and other services making up the balance [S3/F58]. In the audited segment note the hotel segment generated IDR363.7bn of revenue and IDR69.7bn of operating profit, while the real-estate segment generated a small revenue line and an operating loss, so the group's profit is almost entirely a rooms, food and beverage story [S2/F13][S2/F14]. That matters for the valuation: the listed equity is a leveraged play on a handful of luxury properties, not a diversified hotel operator.

Strategy is rate-led and development-heavy. Management states that it focuses on RevPAR growth and, within it, on raising the average daily rate across a premium portfolio that prioritises privacy and luxury; RevPAR grew 6.2% in FY2025 and the two flagship Bali properties were ranked second against their chosen competitor sets [S3/F41]. The 2026 budget continues that approach, targeting occupancy of 62.2% and star-rated hotel revenue growth of 6.1% [S3/F16][S3/F17]. On top of the trading hotels sits a development programme funded by the October 2026 rights issue: the West Resort land at Uluwatu, the Uluwatu Estate infrastructure around it, a Bintan Land tourism development and a full renovation of Alila Ubud [S4/F25][S4/F28][S4/F29][S4/F30][S4/F53][S4/F54].

The company is a challenger in scale, not a leader. It owns a handful of high-rate properties in a destination with thousands of rooms and no ownership of the Alila brand, which was divested by an affiliated company in 2018; the hotels pay management and licence fees that reached IDR19.2bn in FY2025 [S2/F60][S3]. Its edge is location and asset quality — the Uluwatu cliffs and the Ubud river valley — rather than distribution, brand ownership or cost leadership. The moat is therefore narrow and reversionary: it depends on the brand partner's pricing power and on planning scarcity in south Bali, neither of which the company controls.

The controlling shareholder is NUI, which held 61.6% at the end of FY2025 and has been the major and controlling shareholder since 2023; the annual report names Hapsoro as the ultimate beneficial owner, and the press names him as Happy Hapsoro (Hapsoro Sukmonohadi) [S3/F37][S3/F55] [S3/F70][S7]. The public held the rest. The group relationship is central to how this name trades: NUI led the two rights issues, the controller and his vehicles act as standby buyers, and the group's capital-markets agenda — asset injections, development funding and the free-float regime — is a bigger determinant of the twelve-month price than the hotel cash flow [S4][S5].

Bali is the revenue geography. Foreign tourist arrivals to the island reached 4.59m visits in the first eight months of 2026, down 1.6% from the same period a year earlier, according to the provincial statistics office [S9/F45][S9/F46]. Australia remained the largest source market, followed by China and India, and the decline came even as the national picture improved: foreign arrivals to Indonesia reached 10.58m visits in the same period, up 5.4% [S9][S10/F48][S10/F49]. The gap is the industry's central fact for this company — Bali is losing share within Indonesia's inbound tourism even as the country's arrivals grow.

Domestic demand partly offsets that. Domestic trips to Bali reached 18.16m trips in the first eight months of 2026, up 2.1%, although the growth came from intra-provincial movement while inter-provincial trips from outside Bali fell [S9/F47][S9/F64]. The luxury segment in which BUVA operates depends more on foreign high-end travellers and on the Australian, Chinese and Indian markets than on domestic volume, so the domestic offset is only partial; the company's own occupancy slipped from 63.3% in FY2024 to 60.5% in FY2025 even as room rates rose [S3/F1][S3/F2].

The company's trading performance is therefore a rate story in a flat-to-soft volume market. FY2025 revenue rose 5.7% because the average room rate rose, not because occupancy improved, and food and beverage and other revenue added 8.5% [S3/F15][S3/F40]. The 2026 budget assumes occupancy recovers to 62.2% and hotel revenue grows 6.1%, which is a modest recovery assumption against the arrival data rather than an aggressive one [S3/F16][S3/F17]. Our base case takes the budget at face value and then holds growth below it once the renovation drag fades.

Competition is local and brand-led. The annual report benchmarks Alila Villas Uluwatu against five competitor hotels and Alila Ubud against six, ranking second in both, which is a credible position in the Uluwatu and Ubud luxury sets but not evidence of pricing power over the whole island [S3]. New supply in south Bali, the recovery of other Indonesian destinations and the pricing of international luxury chains are the relevant competitive threats; the company does not disclose market share by revenue or rooms, so we treat its position as a niche participant rather than a share leader [S3].

The five-forces read is mixed. Buyer power is high: luxury guests book through global distribution and can substitute to another island or another property within a season, and the company does not own the brand that attracts them. Supplier power is high too: land in Uluwatu is scarce and expensive, labour costs are rising, and the brand partner charges management and licence fees that were IDR19.2bn in FY2025 [S2/F60]. The threat of new entrants is moderate because planning and land access are hard, but the threat of new luxury supply from established operators is real. Substitutes are other destinations — Thailand, Vietnam, the Maldives — and other Bali properties. Rivalry is intense within the luxury set. The result is a business with high gross margins and structurally high operating costs, which is exactly the shape the accounts show.

Regulation and external influences act through three channels. First, tourism policy: visa, airlift and source-market conditions set arrivals, and the provincial data show the destination currently underperforming the country [S9][S10]. Second, the currency: luxury room rates in Bali are effectively priced against the US dollar while most costs are in rupiah, so a weaker rupiah helps the revenue line and a stronger one squeezes it; the macro deck's path is for a mildly weaker rupiah, but the company does not disclose its currency mix [S0]. Third, the capital-market regime: the exchange's free-float rules and MSCI's consultation on Indonesia's classification affect the premium on concentrated- ownership names independently of the hotel cycle, and we treat them as regime risk in sections five and six rather than as industry demand [S0].

The last four years tell a clear story. Revenue rose from IDR225.9bn in FY2022 to IDR371.3bn, then IDR355.3bn and IDR375.6bn; EBITDA moved from IDR26.3bn to IDR55.5bn, IDR122.6bn and IDR109.2bn; attributable profit went from a large loss in FY2022 to IDR35.4bn, IDR8.5bn and IDR99.2bn [S0][S2]. The recovery is real, but the year-on-year profit line is distorted by associate accounting and by non-recurring items, so the EBITDA and operating-profit paths are the better guide to the underlying business.

FY2025 revenue grew 5.7%, driven by higher average room rates, while cost of revenue rose slightly faster and gross profit reached IDR263.0bn [S2][S3/F15]. Gross margin held at about seventy per cent. Reported operating profit nevertheless fell 8.1% to IDR61.6bn, because general and administrative costs rose; the management discussion names that cost line explicitly [S3/F65][S3]. The model's derived EBIT of IDR64.9bn is EBITDA less D&A and is used for forecasting, not as a restatement of the reported line. The company also booked an impairment of IDR4.1bn against properties under development, a reminder that not all of the development spend is productive [S2/F62].

The profit line is the issue. Finance costs were IDR40.1bn, and the associate line swung from a loss in FY2024 to a gain of IDR79.4bn in FY2025 because half-owned associate PT Bukit Savanna Raya sold its Labuan Bajo land and hotel project for IDR799.1bn [S2/F11][S2/F12]. The company itself attributes the 924.5% rise in net profit mainly to that associate profit [S3/F67]. Strip it out and pre-tax profit was a small operating number after interest, not the IDR102.5bn reported [S2]. We therefore exclude the associate gain from the base case: it is a realised asset sale, not a recurring income stream, and the associate's carrying value is already in the balance sheet.

Cash flow is respectable but does not match the profit. Operating cash flow was positive but below the net profit of IDR99.8bn, because the associate gain is non-cash; cash conversion was roughly two-thirds [S2]. Capital expenditure on fixed assets and right-of-use assets was IDR15.0bn, and free cash flow before financing was positive [S2/F42][S2]. Investing cash flow was heavily negative because the company paid IDR536.2bn for nearly all of PT Bukit Permai Properti in November 2025, mostly land and properties under development, and financing cash flow was positive because of the PMHMETD I rights issue [S2/F31][S3]. That is the capital-allocation pattern: raise equity, buy land, develop, and fund the interest bill from operations.

The owner-earnings bridge makes the gap explicit. Attributable profit was IDR99.2bn; adding back D&A of IDR44.3bn and the non-cash associate gain of IDR79.4bn, and subtracting maintenance capex of IDR15.0bn and the working-capital movement, gives a cash figure well above the reported profit, before interest and tax; the model's FCFF is IDR-34.2bn [S2/F11][S2/F42][S2/F56][S0]. For FY2026E the model carries capex of IDR18.0bn against D&A of IDR47.1bn, so net reinvestment is negative and the forecast growth is not manufactured by capital: it comes from room rates and the renovation recovery. That is also why we do not normalise operating capex toward the full D&A charge; the development and renovation spend is funded from the rights proceeds and carried in the bridge at cost, so charging it again as operating capex would double count [S4/F24-F29]. The trade-off is that the equity story depends on the conversion of that bridge, which the bear case now stresses.

The balance sheet at the end of FY2025 showed total assets of IDR2,610.0bn, cash of IDR285.3bn, non-current bank loans of IDR411.5bn plus current maturities and third-party loans, and total equity of IDR2,053.8bn [S2/F33][S2/F34][S2/F35][S2/F36]. Net debt was IDR187.6bn, or 1.7x EBITDA, which is comfortable for a hotel owner [S0]. The latest archived interim is the 30 April 2026 statement reproduced in the rights-issue prospectus, with cash of IDR221.8bn and total liabilities of IDR569.3bn; the net debt carried into the valuation is consistent with that statement and with the data pack's next balance-sheet date [S4/F77][S4/F78][S0]. The equity number flatters the return on capital: it includes a fixed-asset revaluation surplus of IDR1,174.2bn, so reported book value is well above the pre-revaluation base and we do not use P/BV as a valuation method [S2/F68].

The balance sheet has been recapitalised since. PMHMETD II issued 6.15bn new shares at an exercise price of Rp250 a share, raising IDR1,538.6bn gross and taking the share count to 30,771m; the maximum dilution was a fifth of the enlarged capital [S4/F20][S4/F21][S4/F22][S4/F23]. The proceeds are allocated to the early repayment of the Bank Mandiri principal (IDR417.8bn), the Alila Ubud renovation (IDR150.0bn), the RUR acquisition (IDR199.3bn) and capital injection (IDR227.1bn), the Bintan Land development (IDR150.0bn) and Uluwatu Estate infrastructure (IDR390.3bn) [S4/F24-F29]. The company's 2026 budget assumes total equity of IDR3,264.2bn, which is consistent with the recapitalisation [S3/F44].

Our forecasts anchor on the company's own 2026 budget and then fade toward the last actual. FY2026E revenue is IDR398.6bn, the budget line, with EBITDA of IDR96.6bn and a margin of 24.2%; the margin is below FY2025 because the budget's profit target of IDR20.8bn implies a heavier operating-cost load during the Alila Ubud renovation [S3/F18][S3/F19][S4/F25]. The derivation uses the model's FY2026 interest charge of IDR30.6bn - the FY2026 rate on FY2025 closing debt - together with the FY2025 D&A ratio and the effective tax rate; on those inputs the company's own budget implies an EBITDA decline year on year, which we take at face value rather than correcting. Attributable profit is IDR20.9bn, close to the company's target, and EPS is 0.68. From FY2027E revenue growth fades: it holds at five per cent in FY2027E, slows to 4.0% through the phased renovation implementation that runs from Q2 2028 to Q2 2031, then returns to five per cent, lifting EBITDA to IDR132.0bn [S4/F74]. The cost ratio stays above the FY2025 actual through FY2030E and returns to it only in FY2031E, when the renovation completes; maintenance capex is held at about 4.5% of revenue, and no dividend is assumed because the entire proceeds are committed to development and the company has not paid a dividend in the archived record [S3/F52][S4].

Earnings quality. The accruals ratio is low in each of the last three years, so earnings are not outrunning cash in the ordinary sense; the problem is composition, not accrual intensity [S0][S2]. The flagged items are the associate gain, which is a disclosed one-off rather than a fabricated number; the FY2024 other operating income of IDR15.3bn, which flattered that year's base; and the revaluation surplus in equity, which is an accounting uplift rather than cash [S2/F11][S2/F61][S2/F68]. On the desk's classification these are optics-class flags, not manipulation-class: every item is disclosed, audited and traceable, and the auditor issued an unqualified opinion [S3/F50]. The structure flags are more relevant to the equity story than the P&L flags: two rights issues in two years, a large block of HMETD taken by standby buyers, four trading suspensions in 2025 after cumulative price rises, and a controlling shareholder that is also the largest buyer in the recapitalisation [S3/F51][S4][S5].

Working capital is negative, as is normal for hotels that collect deposits and pay suppliers on terms: the model holds operating working capital at about -12.3% of revenue, and the change in working capital is a modest cash inflow as revenue grows [S0]. Capital allocation has been land-heavy and equity-funded; the return on that capital will only be visible once Uluwatu Estate and West Resort are operating, and no source gives us a room count, rate or yield for either project [S4/F53][S4/F54]. We therefore value the development land at book and the proceeds as cash, and let the bull case carry the conversion upside rather than capitalising it in the base.

We use DCF (FCFF) as the primary method because the company owns long-lived, cash-generative hotel assets whose value is a function of a long stream of room revenue, maintenance capital expenditure and a terminal asset value; a multiples-only approach would import the market's current premium into the fundamental value. We cross-check with EV/EBITDA, the standard hotel transaction and trading metric, which converts enterprise value to equity using the same net debt and the same bridge as the DCF. We give P/E no weight in this name. The engine's P/E applies the peer median to LTM attributable profit, which contains the IDR79.4bn associate one-off, and it does not add the bridge that both other methods include; the resulting cross-check is a construction artefact, not a fair-value estimate. A P/E on clean forward earnings with the bridge added would sit in the same range as the other two methods. Dropping the method is therefore the correction, and it lifts the blend because the old weight had been dragging it down.

The cost of capital is built from the macro deck: a risk-free rate of 7.4%, a mature- market equity risk premium of 4.2%, an Indonesia country risk premium of 2.5%, an unlevered beta of 0.90 from the industry default and a levered beta of 0.94, a pre-tax cost of debt of 9.4% and a marginal tax rate of 22.0% [S0]. That gives a cost of equity of 12.1% and a WACC of 11.9%, inside the house rupiah band; we do not add a liquidity premium because the shares trade enough to pass the desk's liquidity thresholds [S0]. The terminal growth rate is 4.0%, below the deck's long-run nominal GDP path and the house cap.

The DCF produces an enterprise value of IDR1,315.1bn and an equity value of Rp108 a share [S0]. The terminal value is 50.5% of enterprise value, so the valuation is not a multiple-expansion story in disguise. The bridge adds the two things the operating cash flow does not capture: the October rights-issue proceeds of IDR1,538.6bn, which pay down the Mandiri facility and fund the development programme, and the properties under development at book of IDR621.0bn, which are non-operating assets in a DCF of the four trading hotels [S2/F32][S4/F22]. We do not add the future development spend as a separate item because the proceeds that fund it are already counted; adding both would double count. Nor do we mark the land above cost in the base case. The record does contain two sourced market marks: the Labuan Bajo land and hotel project was sold for IDR799.1bn, and the RUR acquisition prices the West Resort land of 3.9 hectares at IDR199.3bn [S2/F12][S4/F26][S4/F30]. Both are transactions in specific parcels with their own permitting and development status, and the annual report does not break the 40.2-hectare land bank into owned, permitted and developable hectares; applying a per-hectare mark across the whole bank would assume every hectare carries the same permissions. Cost is therefore the base-case mark, and the sourced comparables are the evidence that a mark-up is plausible; we do not capitalise it because the parcels are not comparable, and even the bull case carries the land at book.

The associate stake is the one part of the bridge that looks conservative. The engine adds the data pack's associate investments line [S0], which is below the LK's associate carrying value; the BSR associate's own balance sheet shows assets of IDR344.5bn and liabilities of IDR28.8bn at the end of FY2025, so BUVA's half share of net assets is larger than the carrying value [S2/F75][S2/F76]. The carrying value already includes BUVA's share of BSR's FY2025 profit of IDR79.4bn, which includes the Labuan Bajo sale [S2/F11][S2/F12]; the remaining gap is BSR's other assets at book, not a distributable cash claim, and no archived source values them. We hold carrying value and disclose the gap rather than revalue the stake on a private balance sheet.

The cross-check diverges, and the reason is informative. EV/EBITDA applies the peer median of 6.9x to LTM EBITDA and gives Rp89, or -16.9% versus the DCF [S0]. The peer set is not a hand-picked hotel group: it is every LEISURE_TOURISM name in the house IDX master with a computable EV/EBITDA - the twelve names are PZZA, CNMA, JSPT, PTSP, PJAA, MAPB, ENAK, KPIG, KOTA, HRME, GOLF and SHID - the same universe file (coverage/universe/idx_master.csv) that supplies the median [S0]. The median is low because the set contains small, illiquid, low-multiple names; a hotel transaction multiple would be higher, which is one reason the DCF, not the multiple, leads. We carry no weighted P/E; for transparency, on our forecast profit the market price is 462.9x times earnings, which is the cleanest statement of how expensive the equity remains after the rights issue [S0].

The konglo lens is the last step, and it is a regime calculation, not a fundamentals judgement. The price is 3.10 times the current fundamental value of Rp101 a share; measured against the twelve-month fundamental value of Rp113 that the target is built from, the ratio is lower - Rp314 against Rp113. The name is a member of the Hapsoro group but is not on the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list, has no index deletion and no enforcement action in the registry, and its free float is 34.3% against a fifteen-per-cent minimum [S0]. Those are the flags that would speed compression, and none is present; the lens therefore keeps a large share of the premium in the base case, closing 30.0% of the log gap over twelve months. That is a deck assumption about flows and index mechanics, not evidence that the group is supporting the price; the only sourced group action is the NUI and standby commitments to take their HMETD entitlements [S12]. The probability-weighted target is Rp269; the regime scenarios run from Rp159 in the bear case, through Rp251 in the base case, to Rp417 in the bull case [S0]. We give the bear-regime target equal prominence: if the flags turn, the lens closes most of the gap and the target falls to Rp159.

What today's price implies is a large development option. The reverse DCF says the market is pricing revenue growth of 28.0% in the first forecast year, against our 5.0% base, to justify the price on the existing cash flow alone [S0]. The price is also 3.10 times the business value, and the gap cannot be closed by the four hotels' earnings power; it is the price of the pipeline and the group premium, and neither is sourced at a value.

The multiple-survival test fails. The DCF's terminal value is 50.5% of enterprise value and is discounted at the WACC with terminal growth of 4.0%, while the market pays 81.4x times our FY2026E EBITDA against a peer median of 6.9x [S0]. The implied exit multiple inside the DCF is therefore below today's entry multiple, not above it, so the valuation does not rely on multiple expansion. The reinvestment check is unflattering in the other direction: capex is below D&A (the owner-earnings bridge in section three), so net reinvestment is negative and ROIIC is not a meaningful driver; the forecast growth is manufactured by room rates and the renovation recovery, not by capital. With a narrow, reversionary moat - location and the brand partner's pricing power, neither controlled by the company - we fade excess returns to the cost of capital by year ten and keep terminal growth below nominal GDP.

The sensitivity grid shows the DCF's dependence on the cost of capital and terminal growth: a one percentage point change in WACC moves the value per share by roughly the same order as a one point change in terminal growth, and the value stays far below the market price across the grid [S0]. The second grid shows the twelve-month value against revenue growth and gross margin: even the outer cells of that grid - extra growth every year and extra margin together - do not close the gap to the current price [S0]. The conclusion is robust to the usual DCF inputs; it is the market's development option and regime premium, not our cost of capital, that accounts for the difference.
The risks that matter are ordered by how much they can change the twelve-month price, not by how likely they are to appear in a filing.

**Demand and destination risk (likelihood high, impact medium).** Bali foreign arrivals fell 1.6% in the first eight months of 2026 while national arrivals rose 5.4% [S9/F46][S10/F49]. If the destination keeps losing share, occupancy and rates come under pressure and the company's rate-led model loses its main lever; the 2026 occupancy target of 62.2% would be hard to meet [S3/F16].

**Execution and renovation risk (likelihood high, impact medium).** The Alila Ubud renovation runs from preparation in Q4 2026, with phased implementation from Q2 2028 to Q2 2031, and the company has not disclosed how many rooms will be offline in each phase [S4/F25][S4/F74]. A longer or more disruptive renovation depresses revenue and margins; the base case trims revenue growth during the implementation years and aligns the SG&A recovery with completion, but it does not assume a full closure because the record says the work is phased.

**Development-conversion risk (likelihood medium, impact high).** Uluwatu Estate infrastructure is due by Q4 2028, West Resort by Q4 2029, and the RUR acquisition is targeted for December 2026 [S4/F53][S4/F54]. The projects have no disclosed room count, rate or return, so the market's premium is an option on management's ability to convert land into income; a delay or a cost overrun would compromise the only part of the equity story that can justify the price. This is the dominant value block: the bridge of rights proceeds and development land is most of the fundamental value, so a write-down lands on the equity in proportion to the haircut. The company already impaired properties under development in FY2025, which is the sourced evidence that the risk is live [S2/F62].

**Dilution and rights-issue risk (likelihood realised, impact medium).** PMHMETD II increased the share count by a quarter and left a large block of HMETD to the standby buyers, with NUI committing to take up its entitlement and transfer part of it [S4/F20][S4/F23][S5][S8]. At the 22 October exercise report 1.88bn HMETD remained unexercised and the four standby buyers had committed to absorb them; the allotment is due on 4 November 2026 [S12/F71][S12]. The equity is now larger and better funded, but the per-share claim on future profits is smaller; a third rights issue would repeat the pattern.

**Governance and related-party risk (likelihood medium, impact high).** NUI controls the company, the controller's vehicles are standby buyers, and the company has acquired land and development assets inside the group's orbit [S3/F37][S4][S5]. The BPP acquisition was a material transaction (properties under development plus goodwill) and the company says it involved no conflict of interest [S2/F31][S3]. The risk is not a disclosed breach; it is the structural ability to buy, sell and fund at prices that favour the group.

**Liquidity and price-volatility risk (likelihood high, impact medium).** The shares were suspended four times in 2025 after cumulative price rises, and the price has moved from Rp2,170 to Rp314 over the past year [S3/F51][S0]. A thin float and a concentrated register mean the exit price can move far from fundamental value in either direction.

**Regime risk (likelihood medium, impact high for the premium).** MSCI opened a consultation on moving Indonesia to Standalone status, with feedback to April 2027 and a decision by June 2027; the exchange has raised the minimum free float and removed high-concentration names from the main indices [S0]. BUVA is not on the HSC list and its float is compliant, so the direct flag is absent, but a market-wide de-rating of Indonesian small caps would compress the premium the lens currently preserves.

**Financial risk (likelihood low, impact medium).** The Mandiri repayment and the rights proceeds reduce net debt, and net debt/EBITDA was 1.7x at FY2025 [S0][S4/F24]. The residual risk is that the development programme consumes the proceeds faster than the projects generate cash, forcing new debt or equity; there is no sourced project cash-flow schedule to test that.

The business scenarios are mirrored on the same three drivers. The bear case is the development write-down and cost-overrun case: revenue growth is cut, gross margin is cut and the SG&A ratio is raised by the mirrored amounts, reflecting a weaker Bali destination as well as an over-budget programme; the bull case adds the same amounts back, reflecting a demand recovery and on-time, on-budget conversion. The probability-weighted fundamental value is Rp113, with the bear at Rp103, the base at Rp113 and the bull at Rp125 [S0]. The engine carries the bridge at cost in every scenario, so a direct haircut is not a separate shock; the bear's operating stress is sized to move the fundamental by an amount of the same order as a haircut on the development block, and a haircut applied directly to the bridge would reduce the fundamental in proportion to the haircut. The scenarios are business scenarios only; the regime scenarios are separate and are what the lens applies to each of them.

The konglo regime scenarios matter more for the twelve-month price than the business scenarios. In the base regime the lens closes 30.0% of the log gap and the target is Rp251; in the bear regime it closes 70.0% and the target falls to Rp159; in the bull regime the premium is allowed to widen, and the target rises to Rp417 [S0]. The dated regime catalysts are the exchange free-float deadline in March 2027, the MSCI consultation feedback deadline in April 2027 and the MSCI decision by June 2027 [S0]. None of them is name-specific today, which is why the base case keeps most of the premium; all of them are market-wide and could change the lens quickly.

Signposts that would change our view. On the fundamental side: a sourced project value for Uluwatu Estate or West Resort (room count, rate, cost and opening date), a sustained recovery in Bali arrivals, or a re-rating of the rupiah that lifts dollar-linked room rates. On the price side: a further collapse toward fundamental value would turn the lens positive, while a new group asset injection or a change of control at a premium would be a separate event requiring a mandatory tender offer, not a fundamentals upgrade. We monitor the monthly foreign-arrival series, the company's quarterly occupancy and rate disclosures, and every material related-party announcement.

Control is concentrated and stable. NUI held 61.6% of the shares at the end of FY2025 and has been the major and controlling shareholder since 2023, when it acquired its stake; the annual report names Hapsoro as the ultimate beneficial owner, and the press names him as Happy Hapsoro (Hapsoro Sukmonohadi) [S3/F37][S3/F55][S3/F70][S7]. After the October rights issue NUI remains the controller; at the 22 October exercise report it held 15.03bn shares while 1.88bn HMETD were still unexercised, with the four standby buyers committed to absorb them [S12/F73][S12/F71][S12]. The registry free float of 34.3% is the pre-exercise figure; if the standby buyers take the remainder the controller and allied holdings rise and the float falls, but the fully exercised pro-forma count of 30,771.32bn shares still leaves the public far above the fifteen-per-cent minimum, so no free-float or HSC flag changes [S12][S4/F23][S0]. The allotment is due on 4 November 2026 [S12]. The name is not on the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list, has no index deletion and no enforcement action in the registry [S0].

The board is small. The annual report lists a president commissioner, one independent commissioner and one further commissioner, with Satrio as president director and Hendry Utomo as director and finance lead; the audit committee, internal audit and corporate secretary functions are in place [S3]. The auditor is Tanubrata Sutanto Fahmi Bambang & Rekan, which issued an unqualified opinion on the FY2025 consolidated statements; the audit fee and the auditor's other services are disclosed, and we found no auditor down-tier change in the record [S3/F50]. Board independence is thin relative to the control block — one independent commissioner out of three — which is a governance weakness rather than a breach.

Related-party dealings are disclosed and mostly structural. The group reports no routine related-party revenue, but it pays management and licence fees of IDR19.2bn, holds modest related-party receivables, and had repaid the related-party loan balance by the end of FY2025 [S2][S2/F60]. The BPP acquisition was a material transaction at IDR536.2bn and the annual report states that no conflict-of-interest transaction took place in the year [S2/F31][S3]. We treat the absence of a disclosed conflict as a positive but not as proof that the group's asset dealings are at arm's length; the relevant test is the price paid relative to an independent valuation, and the archived record does not contain one.

Pledged shares: neither the annual report nor the rights-issue prospectus discloses a pledge of the controlling stake, and the registry shows no enforcement event [S3][S4][S0]. We record the absence rather than infer safety; a pledge would be disclosed under the exchange's ownership-reporting rules and none appears in the record we could archive.

The structure flags are the ones the desk's earnings-quality card asks about. Two rights issues in two years increased the share count materially and transferred a large block of HMETD to standby buyers [S3/F38][S4/F20][S4/F23][S5]. The balance sheet carries a revaluation surplus of IDR1,174.2bn in equity, so reported book value is not a cash-based measure and we do not use P/BV [S2/F68]. The shares were suspended four times in 2025 after cumulative price rises, which is a market-integrity flag under the exchange's rules rather than a company disclosure failure [S3/F51]. The dividend record is nil: no dividend was declared for the year, and the development programme has first claim on cash [S3/F52].

On ESG, the annual report describes an environmental programme centred on the resorts' energy use and emissions, with energy consumption reported lower than the prior year and a sustainability committee in place; the company's positioning as an eco-friendly developer is central to the Alila brand promise and to planning support in Bali [S3]. The main ESG exposure is physical and social: water use and waste in a water-stressed destination, community and land issues around the Uluwatu and Bintan developments, and labour practices in a low-wage service sector. The archived record does not quantify these beyond the energy and emissions metrics, so we treat them as unquantified risks rather than scored factors.

The dated catalysts are the HMETD allotment on 4 November 2026, the Mandiri repayment in late November 2026, the targeted RUR closing in December 2026, the FY2026 results in March 2027, the exchange free-float deadline and the MSCI consultation feedback in the first half of 2027, and the Uluwatu Estate and West Resort completion targets in 2028 and 2029 [S12][S3][S4][S0]. The allotment settles the post-exercise share count and float; the repayment and the RUR closing can change the fundamental story this year; the MSCI events are the ones that can change the premium.

The KPIs we monitor between updates are the quarterly occupancy, average daily rate and RevPAR disclosures, the monthly Bali foreign-arrival series from the provincial statistics office, the company's revenue and profit against its own budget, the completion of the HMETD exercise and the final share count, the RUR conditions precedent, the Alila Ubud renovation timetable, and any recurrence of associate income [S3][S9][S4]. We also watch for related-party announcements, changes in the HSC list or index membership, and any tender offer that would set a floor under the price.

What would change the call. A sourced project value [S0][S4] that lifts the fundamental value toward the market price, or a price decline toward the fundamental value, would move us toward a less negative rating; a new equity issue, a related-party asset purchase at a premium, or a regime decision that accelerates compression would move us further negative. The base case is not a permanent bearish stance: it is the most likely path for a small, group-controlled luxury hotel owner whose current price already discounts a successful development programme.

base.narrative: The company's 2026 revenue and profit budgets are met, Bali arrivals stop falling and the luxury ADR-led pricing holds, the phased Alila Ubud renovation runs to its Q2 2031 completion with revenue growth trimmed and the SG&A ratio recovering only then, and the rights-funded development land is carried at book because the sourced marks are for different parcels; the four trading hotels are valued on their own cash flow.

bear.narrative: The development block is where the value is, so the bear stresses it: the proceeds-funded Uluwatu Estate, West Resort and Bintan Land programme runs over budget and a write-down follows, as the company already impaired properties under development in FY2025 [S2/F62]. Bali arrivals keep falling and the luxury segment underperforms at the same time: revenue growth runs three points below the base path, gross margin is 1.5pp lower and the SG&A ratio is two points higher as the renovation and overrun costs load. Mirrored with the bull on the same three drivers; no extra haircut and no unsourced cost shock.

bull.narrative: Bali arrivals recover toward the national growth rate, the Uluwatu Estate and West Resort conversion stays on the sourced timetable and on budget, and ADR-led pricing lifts revenue growth three points above the base with gross margin 1.5pp higher and the SG&A ratio two points lower as the renovation runs efficiently. Mirrored with the bear on the same three drivers; the development value still sits at cost in the bridge, not as an unsourced project mark-up.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

konglo.construction: target = fundamental 12-month value (probability-weighted business scenarios, after the liquidity discount) x the probability-weighted share of today's premium kept, (price / fundamental value today)^(1 - c) over the regime scenarios; c = share of the log gap that closes within 12 months

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is the company's own budget: revenue target Rp398.629bn against FY2025 revenue of Rp375.584bn [S3/F18][S2/F7], i.e. the +6.14% star-rated hotel revenue target it states [S3/F17] carried at the total-revenue line. FY2027E holds 5%: Bali foreign arrivals were down 1.62% in January-August 2026 while national arrivals grew 5.38% [S9/F46][S10/F49], domestic trips to Bali grew 2.15% [S9/F47], and the company's own plan is occupancy of 62.19% in 2026 [S3/F16] with ADR-led growth. FY2028E-FY2030E are trimmed to 4% because the Alila Ubud renovation implementation runs from Q2 2028 to Q2 2031 and is phased [S4/F74], taking part of the 74-room property's inventory out of service; FY2031E returns to 5% as the renovation completes, then 4% long run, below the deck's Indonesia nominal GDP path. No new hotel opens in the forecast window with a sourced room count: Uluwatu Estate infrastructure is due by Q4 2028 [S4/F53] and West Resort by Q4 2029 [S4/F54], so their future room revenue is not modelled as unsourced capacity.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: Held at the FY2025 actual of 70.03% (gross profit Rp263.03bn on revenue Rp375.58bn [S2/F7]); cost of revenue grew 7.74% in FY2025, broadly in line with revenue [S3], and there is no sourced input-cost shock in the record. The company's F&B revenue rose 8.5% [S3/F40], which supports the mix. Held flat through FY2030E and in the long run.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is solved from the company's own 2026 profit target of Rp20.809bn [S3/F19] on the target revenue of Rp398.629bn [S3/F18], using the model's FY2026 interest charge of Rp30.60bn (the FY2026 rate on FY2025 closing debt), the FY2025 D&A ratio and the 4.5% effective tax rate: it implies SG&A of about 57.6% of revenue and an EBITDA margin of about 24%, 4.8pp below FY2025. That is consistent with the sourced cost trend -- FY2025 operating profit fell 8.09% on 5.72% revenue growth because G&A rose [S3/F65][S3/F15] -- and with the Alila Ubud renovation. The recovery is aligned with the sourced timetable, not with an unsourced schedule: the ratio stays above the FY2025 actual through FY2030E and returns to 52.76% in FY2031E, when the phased renovation implementation that runs from Q2 2028 to Q2 2031 completes [S4/F74]. The long-run ratio is the FY2025 actual, not a squeeze; the drift is a sourced renovation-cycle path and is justified in qc_justifications.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 depreciation and amortisation of Rp44.344bn [S2/F56] over revenue of Rp375.584bn [S2/F7] = 11.81%; the data pack already carries the full LK charge (no restatement), and the ratio is held because the renovation and new infrastructure add depreciable assets only as they are completed.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Maintenance capex only: FY2025 additions to fixed assets were Rp14.956bn plus Rp2.004bn of right-of-use additions [S2/F42], about 4.5% of revenue; FY2024 additions were Rp19.914bn [S2], so the two-year average is close to the same ratio. The development programme (RUR/West Resort, Bintan Land, Uluwatu Estate and the Alila Ubud renovation) is funded from the October 2026 rights issue and carried in the valuation bridge at cost, not double-counted as operating capex; normalising operating capex toward the full D&A charge would charge the renovation and development again while their cost is already the bridge mark. The owner- earnings bridge in section three shows reported profit to FCFF with this split.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 operating working capital was a negative Rp46.34bn (customer advances and payables exceed receivables and inventory) = -12.34% of revenue; hotel operations carry negative working capital, and the ratio is held.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: The FY2024 effective rate was 4.54% (tax Rp0.46bn on pre-tax profit Rp10.20bn) and FY2025 2.69% [S2]; the hospitality final-tax regime and the group's loss position keep the cash tax low. 4.5% is the last clean year and is held.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 finance costs of Rp40.058bn on opening debt of Rp618.849bn = 6.47%; the rate is held. The forecast keeps gross debt at the balance-sheet level in the P&L while the rights-issue proceeds are shown in the valuation bridge: the Bank Mandiri principal repayment of Rp417.8bn occurs in November 2026 [S4/F24], so the interest saving accrues after the balance-sheet date and is reflected in the bridge cash, not as a pre-payment interest forecast.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: FY2025 finance income of Rp2.756bn on opening cash of Rp248.908bn = 1.11%; held at 1.1%.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No new borrowing assumed: the company is repaying rather than drawing debt, and the rights issue is the stated funding source [S4/F24]. The repayment itself is shown in the bridge so that the gross proceeds are not netted twice.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Zero in the forecast. FY2025's Rp79.42bn associate profit [S2/F11] came from the sale of the Labuan Bajo land and hotel project by 50%-owned associate PT Bukit Savanna Raya for Rp799.07bn [S2/F12]; it is a one-off realisation, not a recurring associate stream, and is excluded from the base case rather than capitalised.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minorities took 0.56% of FY2025 net profit and 13.2% of FY2024; 1% is used, reflecting the small, mostly wholly-owned structure (AIM/BPP 99.99%, BLV 99.94%, DMS 99.53%, Culina 50.24%) [S2].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Zero. The company paid no dividend in FY2023-FY2025 [S3/F52] and the entire PMHMETD II proceeds are committed to development and debt repayment [S4/F24][S4/F29]; the dividend policy is left to the AGMS [S3]. No dividend is assumed during the development cycle.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: FY2026E +25%: PMHMETD II issued 6,154,263,660 new shares for 24,617,054,642 old shares (four old for one HMETD at Rp250) [S4/F20][S4/F21][S4/F23], taking the count to 30,771,318,302. No further issuance is assumed after that; the authorised capital allows 50bn new shares but the company has not announced another corporate action.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 4%, below the macro deck's Indonesia long-run nominal GDP path and within the house IDR cap of 5%; Bali luxury hospitality is a mature destination business, not a volume-growth story.

challenges.challenge: The P/E cross-check omits the Rp2,159.6bn bridge (rights proceeds Rp1,538.6bn plus development land Rp621.0bn) that the DCF and EV/EBITDA methods add, and applies 10.87x to LTM attributable profit of Rp99.2bn that contains the Rp79.4bn associate one-off. That is why P/E is 35 against 89.5 and 109; the report instead attributes the 68% gap to small illiquid peers and the one-off. The 15% weight understates the method blend by roughly 7% (about Rp7/share of fundamental).
challenges.answer: Accepted. The engine's P/E cannot add the bridge or clean the LTM profit, so I removed the 15% P/E weight and reweighted to 60% DCF / 40% EV/EBITDA, re-ran the engine (fundamental 113.5, target 269) and rewrote the divergence paragraph to name the bridge omission and the associate one-off as the cause. The report now says a P/E on clean forward earnings plus the bridge would sit near the other methods.

challenges.challenge: Sixty-seven per cent of the fundamental value (Rp2,159.6bn, Rp70.2/share of Rp105) is unspent rights-issue cash and development land carried at cost, and no business or regime scenario stresses it. The bear case shocks only revenue growth and gross margin, which move the fundamental by about 8%, while the risk that matters most - a write-down or cost overrun on the Rp1,120.8bn of proceeds-funded development (the company impaired Rp4.1bn of properties under development in FY2025, S2/F62) - is absent.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The bear scenario is now the development write-down and cost-overrun case (mirrored revenue, margin and opex shocks), its narrative cites the FY2025 impairment, and section 5 reports the bear fundamental and target and states that a direct bridge haircut reduces the fundamental in proportion. The engine values the bridge at cost in every scenario, so the stress is expressed through the mirrored operating drivers rather than a separate bridge haircut; the report says so explicitly.

challenges.challenge: The report says no archived source values the projects independently and carries the land at cost, but S2 itself contains the market evidence: the Labuan Bajo land and hotel project was sold for Rp799.1bn (S2 p.83) and the RUR acquisition prices 3.9ha of Uluwatu land at Rp199.3bn, about Rp51bn/ha [S4/F26][S4/F30]. A per-hectare mark on the 40.2ha land bank would be several times the Rp621.0bn book and is the largest single bull lever in the file; it is not shown even as a sensitivity.
challenges.answer: Accepted in part. The report now records the sourced marks (BSR land and hotel sale; RUR West Resort land price and hectares), explains that they are specific parcels with different permissions, and states that the annual report does not split the land bank into owned, permitted and developable hectares. Cost stays the base mark and the report explains why the sourced comparable is not applied across the bank; even the bull case carries the land at book. I did not fabricate a per-hectare sensitivity the record cannot support.

challenges.challenge: The model grows revenue 5% a year from FY2027 while Alila Ubud, 74 of 301 rooms, is in full renovation from Q4 2026 to Q2 2031 [S4/F25]. It also recovers the opex ratio to the FY2025 level by FY2030, a year before the renovation ends. Either the renovation removes rooms and revenue, or it does not load costs; the model takes the cost drag but none of the revenue loss, and neither the revenue path nor the recovery timetable is sourced.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The prospectus timetable is now sourced as pre-construction from Q4 2026 to Q2 2028 and phased implementation from Q2 2028 to Q2 2031; revenue growth is trimmed during implementation and the SG&A recovery returns to the FY2025 ratio only in FY2031. The report states the EBITDA effect of the slower growth and later recovery.

challenges.challenge: The post-balance-sheet review says 1.87bn HMETD remained unexercised at the 25 October report and cites [S10], which is the Antara BPS foreign-arrivals article; the 25 October source is nowhere in the archive. It also refers to a 30 June 2026 balance sheet while the only archived interim is 30 April 2026 (S4 p.53), which is where the 224.4 net debt and 221.8 cash appear to come from. The figure and the date are load-bearing for the dilution risk and the bridge.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Archived the 25 October Kontan report as S12 (the fetcher could not parse the gzip-wrapped page, so the extracted article text is stored and registered); all HMETD claims now cite S12 and the S10 citation is corrected. The post-balance-sheet note and section 3 restate the latest interim as 30 April 2026, with cash and liabilities cited to S4.

challenges.challenge: The investment summary and section 4 say the price is 3.36x the twelve-month fundamental value, but 314/104.88 is 2.99x. The 3.357 lens ratio is price divided by the current fundamental value of Rp93.5 (the twelve-month value discounted one year at COE). The report overstates the premium by 12% at the exact point where it explains the thesis.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The report now labels 3.36x as price divided by current fundamental value (3.10x after the re-run) and shows the twelve-month ratio as the price against the twelve-month fundamental, with the same correction in the investment summary.

challenges.challenge: VAL_COMPOUNDER_QUALITY requires the reinvestment rate, ROIIC, fade year and implied exit multiple versus entry multiple. The report gives only the terminal-value share (50%) and asserts the multiple-survival test fails without a number. Growth is declared, not manufactured: capex of 4.5% of revenue against D&A of 11.8% is negative net reinvestment, so the 5% revenue and 4% terminal growth have no stated capital source and no fade evidence.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Added the reinvestment-rate and ROIIC discussion: capex is below D&A, so net reinvestment is negative and ROIIC is not a meaningful driver; growth comes from rates and the renovation recovery. Added the multiple-survival test with the DCF terminal-value share and the market EV/EBITDA versus the peer median, and stated the year-ten fade and narrow moat.

challenges.challenge: The opex path lifts SG&A from the FY2025 actual 52.76% to 57.6% in FY2026 and steps it back to exactly 52.76% by FY2030 (57.6/56.0/54.8/53.8/52.76) with no source for the shape, only the endpoint and the renovation narrative. In the opposite direction, capex at 4.5% of revenue versus D&A of 11.8% means FCFF is 82% of EBITDA for a portfolio of trophy resorts; the owner-earnings bridge that would show whether that is maintenance or underinvestment is absent.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The opex path now holds above the FY2025 ratio through FY2030 and recovers only at the FY2031 renovation completion, and the owner-earnings bridge runs reported profit to FCFF with the maintenance/growth split argued. I did not normalise capex toward D&A: the development and renovation spend is funded from the rights proceeds and carried in the bridge at cost, so charging it again would double count; the report says so.

challenges.challenge: The free float of 34.27% is the 22 October registry figure, before the HMETD exercise closed. If the controller and the standby buyers take the 1.87bn unexercised HMETD, the group's stake rises toward 68% and the float falls to roughly 28%, so the report's statement that the public holds about a third of the enlarged company is stale. The 86% drawdown from 2,170 to 314 and four 2025 suspensions are listed but not integrated into the regime reading that supports keeping 77% of the premium.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Section 6 now uses the 22 October exercise report: unexercised HMETD, shares issued, the NUI holding, the four standby commitments and the 4 November allotment. The registry float is labelled pre-exercise; the fully exercised pro-forma count still leaves the public well above the 15% floor, so no HSC or float flag changes, and the report integrates the drawdown into the regime reading.

challenges.challenge: The bridge adds Rp66.5bn for all associate stakes, but the FY2025 associate note shows PT Bukit Savanna Raya with net assets of Rp315.7bn (assets 344.5 less liabilities 28.8, S2 p.83); BUVA's 50% economic share is about Rp158bn, roughly Rp3/share above the book mark. The report neither revalues the stake nor explains the gap between equity-method book and the associate's own balance sheet.
challenges.answer: Accepted as a reconciliation. Added the BSR balance-sheet arithmetic: assets, liabilities and the 50% share above the carrying value; the carrying value already includes BUVA's share of the BSR profit including the Labuan Bajo sale, and the remaining gap is BSR's other assets at book, not a distributable cash claim. No source values them, so we hold carrying value and disclose the gap.

challenges.challenge: The only reason given for the 266 target is that the group has an interest in supporting the price during the development programme. That is unsourced, and it is the single input that turns a 67% fundamental discount into a 15.4% expected return. The konglo card requires the report to argue why the base case closes that much of the gap for this name, not to assert group support.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Removed the unsourced sentence that the group has an interest in supporting the price. The lens is now labelled a deck assumption about flows and index mechanics; the only sourced group action is the NUI and standby commitments to take their HMETD entitlements, and the bear-regime target is given equal prominence in the summary.

challenges.challenge: FY2026E EBITDA margin is 24.2% against 29.1% for FY2025A (-4.8pp). The qc_justification says the SG&A ratio was solved at the FY2025 interest charge on the opening debt (Rp40.06bn), but the model actually uses Rp30.60bn, the FY2026 charge on FY2025 closing debt; at Rp40.06bn the solved opex would be about 55.3%, not 57.6%. The target is sourced, so the output is close, but the explanation does not describe the calculation.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Restated the derivation with the interest charge the model actually uses (the FY2026 charge on FY2025 closing debt), not the FY2025 charge on opening debt, and noted that the company's own budget implies an EBITDA decline year on year. The qc justification and section 3 now match the calculation.

challenges.challenge: The report says operating profit fell 8.1% to Rp64.9bn, but the company's own line is Rp61.62bn, down 8.09% from Rp67.04bn [S3/F65]; 8.1% from 67.04 is 61.6, not 64.9. The 64.85 is the model's derived EBIT (EBITDA less D&A) and the 8.09% is the reported figure. challenges.answer: Accepted. Prose now uses the reported operating profit via F69 and explains that the model's derived EBIT is EBITDA less D&A. The UBO claim is cited to the annual-report statement naming Hapsoro (F70) and the press naming him Happy Hapsoro (S7).

challenges.challenge: The EV/EBITDA and P/E cross-checks use peer medians of 6.90x and 10.87x, but the comps screen shows BUVA alone in LEISURE_TOURISM and the peer set is the house universe master, not an archived source. The report's explanation that the median is low because the set contains many small, illiquid names cannot be verified from the record.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Named the peer set behind the EV/EBITDA median: the twelve LEISURE_TOURISM names in the house IDX master with a computable multiple (PZZA, CNMA, JSPT, PTSP, PJAA, MAPB, ENAK, KPIG, KOTA, HRME, GOLF, SHID), sourced to the house universe file; P/E is no longer weighted.

missing_bull_case.note: The bull scenario only adds 3pp revenue growth and 1.5pp gross margin (114 vs base 104), yet the only sourced market values in the record point the other way: BSR sold Labuan Bajo land and a hotel project for Rp799.1bn (S2 p.83) and RUR pays Rp199.3bn for 3.9ha of Uluwatu land (~Rp51bn/ha). The 67% bridge block gets no upside case and the associate's Rp315.7bn net assets are ignored.

missing_bear_case.note: No scenario stresses the dominant value block: a development write-down or cost overrun on the Rp1,120.8bn of proceeds-funded assets (FY2025 already impaired Rp4.1bn of properties under development, S2/F62), the renovation revenue loss at Alila Ubud, or a negative MSCI Standalone decision, which falls by 30 June 2027 and therefore inside the 12-month target window. The risks section names these; the model does not carry them.

assumption_realism.note: Revenue grows 5% a year from FY2027 while Alila Ubud (74 of 301 rooms) is in full renovation to Q2 2031 (S4/F25), and the opex ratio recovers to the FY2025 level by FY2030, a year before the renovation ends. Capex is held at 4.5% of revenue against D&A of 11.8%, so FCFF is 82% of EBITDA and the asset base is never replenished. The volume, renovation and reinvestment assumptions are not mutually consistent.

evidence_and_citations.note: The 1.87bn unexercised HMETD is cited to S10, which is the Antara BPS arrivals article, and the actual 25 October source is not archived. The post-balance-sheet review refers to a 30 June 2026 balance sheet but the archived interim is 30 April 2026 (S4 p.53), and that is where the 224.4 net debt appears to come from. The UBO claim is cited to F37/F55, which do not name Happy Hapsoro. The 6.90x and 10.87x peer medians are unverifiable.

valuation_method_fit.note: The DCF is the right primary and the WACC/COE are in the house band, but the P/E cross-check omits the Rp2,159.6bn bridge that the other two methods include and applies 10.87x to an LTM profit containing the Rp79.4bn one-off (35 vs 89.5 vs 109); the reported explanation of the 68% divergence is therefore wrong. The compounder card's reinvestment-rate, ROIIC and implied-exit-multiple outputs are missing, and the 3.36x is stated against the twelve-month fundamental when it is price/current value of 93.5 (12-month ratio 2.99x).

bias_and_tone.note: The prose is balanced and credits the asset quality, the recapitalisation and the disclosed governance record. But the 266 target rests on one unsourced sentence - that the group has an interest in supporting the price during the development programme - and on the deck's compress. The fundamental (105) versus target (266) gap needs a stronger, dated regime argument than it gets.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: The macro deck drives the cost of capital (rf 7.45%, ERP/CRP, USD/IDR 18,350 vs 18,120 spot) and the 4% terminal growth sits below nominal GDP, inside the 5% IDR cap. LEISURE_TOURISM is a corporate growth-template with dcf_fcff primary at 60% per fund record, and no commodity, royalty or licence parameter applies. The deck read is consistent.

conservatism_audit.note: Opex is held 4.8pp above the FY2025 ratio in FY2026 and steps to exactly the FY2025 ratio by FY2030 on an unsourced path (57.6/56.0/54.8/53.8/52.76), a conservative drift with no sourced shape. In the other direction capex at 4.5% of revenue against 11.8% D&A is an optimistic owner-earnings assumption. Payout zero, no new borrowing and no development contribution are sourced. The mirrored bear/bull shocks are correctly mirrored but reach only the ~33% operating slice, not the 67% bridge.

calibration.note: FY2026E EBITDA margin of 24.2% does not reproduce FY2025A at 29.1% (-4.8pp); the drift.opex_pct BLOCK is answered with the company's own sourced 2026 revenue and profit targets (S3/F18/F19), which is acceptable in principle, but the stated derivation is wrong: it says the FY2025 interest charge on opening debt (Rp40.06bn) was used, while the model uses Rp30.60bn, the FY2026 charge on FY2025 closing debt. At Rp40.06bn the solved opex would be ~55.3%, not 57.6%. No other BLOCK flags; the write-up should say the company budget itself implies an ~11% EBITDA decline.

findings.finding: post_bs_review says the 224.4 net debt comes from the 30 April 2026 statement [S4/F77][S4/F78], but that statement's debt (bank 435.294 + third-party 24.5 + leases 1.412 = 461.206) less cash 221.762 gives 239.4. The 224.4 is the 30 June 2026 data pack (debt 455.130 - cash 230.776 [S0]); C5's restatement of the source is still wrong. Value impact is about Rp0.5 per share (0.4%), so FIX, not BLOCK.

Model FY2025A EBITDA of 109.198 (pack EBIT 64.854 + D&A 44.344) is 4.0% above the company's own FY2025 EBITDA of 105.001 (S4 p.16; reported operating profit 61.618 + D&A 44.344, S2/F69/F56), and FY2024A is 122.607 against 104.860 (+16.9%). The pack EBIT carries other income, so the calibration actual margin of 29.07% overstates the company's 27.96% and the drift justification's 'about eleven per cent' FY2026 EBITDA decline is about 8% on the company's own base. FY2025 is inside the 5% block threshold; the FY2024 line and the decline claim are not right.

The bear is an operating proxy, not a direct development write-down: the engine carries the Rp1,538.6bn proceeds and Rp621.0bn land at cost in every scenario, and the bear's -8.8% move (113 to 103) approximates a 20-30% haircut on the Rp1,120.8bn proceeds-funded block (6.5-9.7% of fundamental). The magnitude claim in section 5 is therefore fair, but the proxy is permanent operating impairment rather than a one-off asset mark, and the scenario narrative should not imply a modelled write-down.

The FY2027E-FY2030E opex glide (56.8/56.0/54.8/53.8%) is an interpolation with no sourced annual shape; the sourced anchors are the FY2026 budget-implied 57.6% and the Q2 2031 renovation completion [S4/F74]. The same prospectus page also says the Alila Ubud renovation is expected to finish by Q4 2028 (S4 p.37) while the detailed timetable runs Q2 2028 to Q2 2031; the model uses the later, conservative end.

Section 4 compares the reverse-DCF implied first-year growth (28.0%) with the FY2027E 5.0% placeholder rather than FY2026E 6.14%, and C6's twelve-month price/fundamental ratio is shown as two numbers (314 against 113) rather than the 2.78x quotient. Both are template labels, not engine mismatches.
